scenes.title: Multi-Region Access Points: global entry and regional data
scenes.visual_overview: The approved slide teaches multi-region access points: global entry and regional data through a service architecture and explanation panels.
visual_walkthrough: Read the global endpoint and its traffic-routing decision toward suitable regional S3 buckets
Distinguish regional request routing from creating or maintaining object replicas
Explain how routing health, access policy and replication setup affect failure recovery
scenes.visual_example: For a global download application, a Multi-Region Access Point can select an available regional path, but cross-Region replication is still independently configured.
scenes.visual_synthesis: One global endpoint does not make every Region contain consistent objects.
scenes.narration: This slide introduces a Multi-Region Access Point, which gives clients a global S3 access endpoint and routes requests toward appropriate regional buckets. Follow the request from the client to the global entry, then inspect the destination regional bucket. That is a routing decision, not automatic creation of a second object copy. If the solution expects identical content in more than one Region, configure and monitor replication separately, and consider its asynchronous lag. Also examine authorization for the multi-region access point and the underlying buckets, because a healthy route is not sufficient when access is denied. Imagine a global document service that wants resilient reads during a regional disruption. Its access-point routing, replication, encryption keys and failover testing must work together. The professional-level choice is whether you need a global request endpoint, independent replicated data, or both. Do not confuse traffic routing with the data-recovery mechanism.

scenes.title: Legacy S3 transforms and Glacier vault retention need context
scenes.visual_overview: The approved slide teaches legacy s3 transforms and glacier vault retention need context through a service architecture and explanation panels.
visual_walkthrough: Separate historical S3 Object Lambda transformation patterns from current support and eligibility constraints
Distinguish original Glacier vault archive concepts from modern S3 Glacier storage classes
Choose a currently supported design for transformation, retention and retrieval rather than copying legacy assumptions
scenes.visual_example: An older architecture may reference Object Lambda for on-the-fly redaction and vault locks for archives; new designs must verify service eligibility and use supported storage or processing alternatives.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Historical service names should not silently determine a modern production architecture.
scenes.narration: This comparison highlights features that older S3 training material may present as universal design choices. First, consider an object transformation path such as S3 Object Lambda. Its historical goal was to change object responses, for example by redacting content before delivery, but current availability and customer eligibility must be verified before selecting it for a new workload. Where it is not suitable, use a supported application or processing tier with equivalent controls. The other side describes older Amazon Glacier vault and vault-lock retention terminology. That history is not interchangeable with the present S3 Glacier storage-class workflow, bucket policies or S3 Object Lock retention. For a compliance archive, specify the actual supported class, minimum retention, permitted administrators and documented restore path. The decision should be made using current service support, rather than an exam diagram whose legacy labels suggest all these interfaces remain equally available.

scenes.title: Presigned URLs delegate a bounded request
scenes.visual_overview: The approved slide teaches presigned urls delegate a bounded request through a service architecture and explanation panels.
visual_walkthrough: Follow the signer issuing a URL tied to a particular S3 operation, object and permitted request
Explain signature expiration, effective signer authorization and temporary credential expiry
Walk a direct upload or download example with careful object naming and application-side validation
scenes.visual_example: An application authorizes an upload and issues a short-lived presigned PUT, but constrains object scope and validates processing before making the new content visible.
scenes.visual_synthesis: A presigned URL delegates the signing principal's bounded request; it is not a public bucket policy.
scenes.narration: This slide follows a request from an authenticated application to S3 without routing all of the object bytes through an application server. A trusted signer creates a presigned URL for a particular operation and object key. The client uses that URL for a direct upload or download within its validity period. Notice the security boundary: the URL conveys authority derived from the signing credentials and the applicable S3 policies; it does not grant more permissions than the signer has. Expiration is bounded by the URL configuration and, when temporary credentials are used, by their actual lifetime. The application should validate the intended key, operation, size or content controls and any post-upload processing steps rather than trusting arbitrary client filenames. For a customer media portal, short-lived signed uploads reduce proxy bandwidth while keeping authorization in the application. Do not treat the URL as an indefinitely reusable secret or an excuse to make the underlying bucket public.

scenes.title: S3 evidence: access logs, data events and metrics
scenes.visual_overview: The approved slide teaches s3 evidence: access logs, data events and metrics through a service architecture and explanation panels.
visual_walkthrough: Distinguish S3 server access logs from CloudTrail object-level data events
Explain the role of request, error and operational metrics as aggregated signals
Choose the right evidence source for audit, diagnosis and cost investigations
scenes.visual_example: A 403 spike suggests an authorization issue; metrics locate the symptom, CloudTrail data events may help identify object API calls and logging can add request context.
scenes.visual_synthesis: No single telemetry source proves every request succeeded or explains its cause.
scenes.narration: This slide compares three evidence sources that answer different operational questions. S3 server access logging provides request records when enabled and properly configured, but delivery behavior and detail should be understood before treating it as an instant audit feed. CloudTrail data events capture supported object-level API activity when those event selectors and destinations are configured; standard management events alone are not a substitute for object data-event coverage. Metrics and dashboards provide aggregated counts, errors and performance trends to help find where an incident is occurring. Imagine an unexpected increase in access-denied requests. Metrics identify the time and affected bucket, while appropriately configured event records and request logs can support investigation of principals, actions and request context. Correlate the information with IAM, bucket and endpoint policies. Select and retain evidence based on the operational, cost and audit requirement; no single chart proves that every object transaction was correct.
